claims.text: Temperature-dependent formation of a protective oxide film controls the onset or suppression of corrosion degradation in Q235 steel.
Elevated temperature accelerates the formation of a coherent, adherent magnetite (Fe3O4) layer on Q235 steel.
The magnetite layer formed at elevated temperature partially shields Q235 steel from further corrosion degradation.
At room temperature, slower oxide growth produces incomplete surface coverage.
Incomplete oxide coverage permits localized corrosion at grain boundaries and inclusions.
As-received Q235 steel contains inclusions and grain-boundary sites relevant to corrosion initiation.
The oxide film consists primarily of magnetite.
The oxide film nucleates preferentially at inclusions and grain boundaries.
Elevated temperature increases ion mobility in the corrosive system.
Faster oxidation and ion transport enable rapid growth of a continuous magnetite film.
A continuous magnetite film slows iron dissolution.
Room-temperature oxidation is too slow to form a fully coherent protective film during the specified comparison.
After identical exposure times, elevated-temperature samples will have lower mass loss than room-temperature samples.
After identical exposure times, elevated-temperature samples will have lower pit density than room-temperature samples.
After identical exposure times, elevated-temperature samples will have a thicker and more uniform Fe3O4 layer than room-temperature samples.
The proposed protection requires dissolved oxygen and chloride conditions that permit stable oxide growth.
Sufficiently aggressive conditions can break down a continuous oxide layer and eliminate its protective effect.
